Late-night hosts weighed in on Trump’s relationship with tech leaders and the White House’s new AI-powered site

On Tuesday night, late-night hosts discussed a Maha summit in Washington DC, the White House’s new AI-powered website and Donald Trump once again falling asleep on live TV.

On NBC, Seth Meyers focused on the president’s ill-phrased announcement of the US murder rate declining. “We have the best, uh, murder,” Trump said.

“What are you talking about, ‘We have the best murder’?” Meyers responded. “It’s a murder rate, not a murder rating.”

On Monday, Trump also took issue with the claim by the US ambassador to China, David Perdue, claim that he offered to sell weapons to China, saying: “I think he was probably talking about Taiwan.”

“So wait, are you saying that we have an ambassador to China who doesn’t know the difference between China and Taiwan?” asked Meyers. “That’s like if Mr Met showed up to the stadium wearing a Yankees jersey.”

Meanwhile, health officials in Florida have issued a local state of emergency after an outbreak of dengue fever. “Man, RFK Jr has only had the job two years and Florida is already turning into an episode of House,” the host laughed.

The White House has also rebuked criticism of taxpayer-funded TV ads. They said “they are public service announcements that are ‘reminding Americans to love their country’”, explained Meyers, before quipping: “The clearest sign of a healthy relationship is if you have to remind someone to love you.”

Trump reportedly told congressional leaders on Friday that he was revoking nearly $1bn in federal funding.

“Oh God, what’s he doing to the reflecting pool now?” joked Meyers. “Is he adding a waterslide?”

Meyers closed his monologue with news that the makers of a smart glasses brand have recalled frames after customers reported them overheating and causing burns.

“Well, I hate to break it to you,” he said, “but no matter what smart glasses you’re wearing, you’re gonna get burned.”

On Jimmy Kimmel Live! the host discussed Trump hosting all the top tech executives at the White House for a lunch on Tuesday. The guest list included Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman and the House speaker, Mike Johnson, “who was there to ask if there was any way that AI could turn him into a real boy”.

In a press conference, Trump announced that he was “changing the name” of AI from “artificial intelligence” to “superintelligence” “So far, everybody likes it,” he added.

“Yes,” responded Kimmel drily. “I’m sure the guy whose company’s name is OpenAI is very excited about this development.

“The idea that our guardrails against AI are being erected by an addled 80-year-old man … It’s like asking your grandpa to set up a wifi router in your house. You just wouldn’t do it.”

The host moved on to talk about the new AI-powered government website America.gov.

“A White House official called America.gov ‘a new front door for the federal government’,” said Kimmel. “You know, we need a new front door because Trump demolished the old front door to build his ballroom.”

Kimmel added that Trump is still trying to blame all of America’s struggles on his predecessor, again branding former president Joe Biden “sleepy” in Oval Office remarks this week. Ironically, Trump fell asleep shortly after.

“Only a few minutes after invoking the name ‘sleepy Joe Biden’, nappy Don Trump drifted off to dreamland on live TV,” Kimmel said.

This week also saw the second annual Maha summit in DC in an event attended by JD Vance, Robert F Kennedy Jr and Mike Tyson.

“You know we’re screwed when the sanest person in the group has half a face tattoo,” Kimmel said.

fullText:
Donald Trump and six tech executives voluntarily signed the document, which included a misspelling, committing to safely developing AI

The White House misspelled “United States” under the signature of Donald Trump on an accord he signed with AI executives on Tuesday.

At the bottom of the accord on “Super Intelligence”, the term Trump has used to rebrand artificial intelligence, the president’s signature appeared as “President of the Unites States”.

It is unclear how the misspelling occurred or whether it will appear in the Federal Register, the database that contains official presidential actions and other government documents.

Trump and six tech executives signed the document voluntarily committing to safely developing AI to address widespread concerns, sparked by industry leaders who warned the technology is evolving too rapidly to control.

Trump has largely brushed aside concerns about AI harming humans and called for companies to continue developing the technology so the US can become the global leader in AI. Even while signing the accord on safety, the US president praised the business executives for growth.

Trump posted the document containing the misspelling on Truth Social, and the White House Communications Team emailed it out shortly after it was signed.

The Bloomberg News correspondent David Gura appeared to be the first to notice the spelling error.

The Guardian has asked the White House for comment

The accord on artificial intelligence outlined four layers of “controls and audits” that companies will implement to ensure AI capabilities operate as intended. That includes “robust” internal controls and partnering with an “independent external auditor or evaluator”.

Potential internal controls could include empowering a team to monitor and detect that AI is operating correctly and creating monitors to ensure AI technologies will not hack or access technical systems in cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats.

External monitors would also check to make sure the AI is operating as intended and companies could designate a committee of the board of directors to oversee reports from teams operating the controls of the AI.

The accord is the first step in addressing concerns, raised by industry experts in mid-September.

Americans have become increasingly skeptical of AI. A recent New York Times/Siena College poll found that 61% of voters opposed the construction of datacenters, while an SSRS/CNN poll found that 71% of Americans believed the government wasn’t doing enough to regulate the growth and development of AI.

While Tuesday’s document is only an accord, it left open the possibility of codifying the framework into formal regulations or laws – something Trump has repeatedly rejected.

“I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing,” Trump told reporters outside the White House on Tuesday. “And they understand that they have to self-police.”

The six executives who signed the accord are Dario Amodei from Anthropic; Elon Musk from SpaceXAI; Greg Brockman from OpenAI; Jensen Huang from Nvidia; Mark Zuckerberg from Meta; and Sundar Pichai from Google.

title: Trump's tariffs are back in court — again
description: Containers are seen at the container terminal of Nanjing Port, in China's eastern Jiangsu province on September 8, 2026. Most Chinese goods shipped to the United States have faced a minimum 12.5% tax. - AFP/Getty...
fullText:
Here we go again: President Donald Trump's sweeping global tariffs are back under the legal microscope.

On Wednesday, a three-judge panel at the US Court of International Trade is set to hear arguments in a case that could determine whether the president can use a 1970s trade law to impose tariffs on nearly everything the United States imports.

Since late July, goods from 80 countries, including China, India and Japan, have faced tariff rates ranging from 10% to 12.5%. The administration imposed the duties after determining that those countries had allegedly failed to address the use of forced labor in producing goods shipped to the US. The US Trade Representative recommended the tariffs as a remedy, with higher rates applying to countries deemed the "worst offenders."

The rollout of these tariffs coincided with the lapse of a separate 10% near-blanket duty Trump had imposed earlier in the year under a different legal authority. The Supreme Court later ruled that Trump had overstepped his authority, which immediately invalidated the tariffs and triggered $168 billion worth of refunds for importers.

The complaint, filed by the Liberty Justice Center, a libertarian public-interest law firm that successfully won the landmark Supreme Court tariff case, argues that the administration is moving to preserve a predetermined global tariff policy. That, they argue, is an improper use of the trade law commonly referred to as Section 301.

Administration officials, meanwhile, told reporters previously that the timing was to "avoid complexity" that would come from layering the new levies on top of the then-10% duties.

"The real message here that everyone needs to take away is the president is going to always use the tools at his disposal to achieve his trade policy objectives," administration officials said on a briefing call with reporters shortly before the 10%-15% duties took effect.

While Wednesday's arguments may offer clues about how the judges view the case, a ruling could still take weeks — if not months. Either side could then appeal the decision to the US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, which could also decide whether to pause enforcement of the tariffs while the case proceeds.

The fight could eventually reach the Supreme Court, extending the legal battle for several months more.

title: GOP Sen. Mike Lee blocks effort to bar Trump from demolishing Kennedy Center
description:
A Republican senator squashed a bipartisan push to prohibit the Trump administration from demolishing the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.
Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Oregon, and Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, who lead the Senate panel that oversees funding for the Kennedy Center, tried to pass a bill that would require an act of Congress to demolish any national memorials that honor a president.
fullText:
A Republican senator squashed a bipartisan push to prohibit the Trump administration from demolishing the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.

Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Oregon, and Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, who lead the Senate panel that oversees funding for the Kennedy Center, tried to pass a bill that would require an act of Congress to demolish any national memorials that honor a president. An objection from a single senator can block a bill from being passed by unanimous consent.

Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, objected.

The bill – dubbed the "Protecting Presidential Memorials Act" – would also apply to Lincoln Memorial and Washington Monument. But Merkley and Murkowski made their immediate goal clear.

"This has of course to do with the president planning to demolish the Kennedy Center," Merkley said on the Senate floor late Monday evening, Sept. 28, after the passing of the Protect College Sports Act, a major overhaul to college athletics related to NIL (name, image and likeliness) payment for student athletes.

Lee's office said in a statement to USA TODAY that this effort should go through "the appropriate committee process."

"Democrats should join us in lowering the cost of living and securing American elections instead of wasting the Senate’s time with partisan scaremongering," Lee said in the statement shared by communications director Billy Gribbin.

The Senate vote is the latest chapter in a year of legal wrangling and congressional wrangling over the Kennedy Center.

The Kennedy Center added Trump's name to the building's facade in December 2025 after the board – which was handpicked by Trump – voted to rename the center. In June 2026, a judge ordered that his name be taken down, saying that an act of Congress was needed to change the name of the memorial to the assassinated president.

Trump's name has since been removed, but a tarp remains covering the building's name where Trump's name used to be.

Earlier in September, the Kennedy Center closed after part of the ceiling collapsed, and on Sept. 15 the center's board voted to close the center for two years.

That came after a federal judge's second ruling that Trump's name could not be added to the building in September 2026, the culmination of months of legal disputes as the president contended that the center needed to be renovated, that only he could raise the money for it and that his administration should be recognized for it.

Trump has continued to defend his stance about his name being on the building, saying on Sept. 18 that the center had "been a dump" and "lost money" for years. He said that he would subsidize the necessary repairs but said that his administration should be recognized.

Merkley accused the president of wanting to demolish the center, pointing to an image captured of Trump inside Air Force One reading a poster that appears to say "Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED." The photo was taken hours after Trump told reporters that the memorial will "end up being ripped down" unless major renovations are undertaken.

title: The US Government Just Launched an AI Chatbot
description: The Trump administration just launched a chatbot for government-related questions.
fullText:
AI is virtually everywhere in 2026; that now includes U.S. government websites. On Tuesday, the Trump administration launched "America.gov," a new website that uses AI to answer questions about the government. While the experience currently feels like ChatGPT running U.S. government-themed instructions, the plan is for America.gov to eventually let you take action as well.

America.gov "combines" the nearly 30,000 websites under the umbrella of the U.S. government into one set of sources. Rather than invite you to browse those tens of thousands of pages to answer your questions, that dataset serves as the basis for the site's proprietary chatbot. You ask the chatbot a question about the U.S. government, and the AI sifts through those websites to generate an answer. It's like ChatGPT, but if the model only had access to U.S. government websites and sources.

You could ask the site how to replace your Social Security card, renew your passport, or register to vote in your state. You could ask for information on changing your address with the USPS, when Medicare open enrollment dates are, or upload a PDF of a government form for assistance. The site says any personal information will be automatically removed, though the privacy policy clarifies that it "will make a best-effort attempt in your browser to remove any private details using Rampart (an open-source classifier system to detect some types of PII, such as Social Security Numbers, phone numbers, email addresses, and credit card numbers)."

The website currently supports three languages—English, Spanish, and French—as well as voice commands, if you prefer speaking to your chatbots rather than typing to them. You don't need an account to use it, nor is there a fee or subscription, and there are no ads.

In its current form, America.gov is a simple chatbot. But the site has bold claims for future features. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced plans to let users apply for and renew their passports directly through the site, including a dynamic progress tracker to keep tabs on your documents. Other future abilities could include enrolling in Medicare or finding a job with the federal government.

But as with all claims, take these with a grain of salt. The government says these features are coming in early 2027, but this is a tall order for such a project. A single website that lets you complete complex government processes with the simplicity of a chatbot sounds great, but it would need to be accurate and reliable for all possible tasks and functions. It would certainly take significant proof of security and dependability for me to trust such a program with renewing my passport or helping me enroll in health care.

It's impossible to discuss America.gov without acknowledging the administration that is spearheading the project. One would assume that an AI-powered government website developed by this administration would be biased towards Trump and his many falsehoods. And yet, the tool is astoundingly neutral, to the point where I can only imagine how frustrated Trump would be by some of these answers.

The first question many tested America.gov with was "Who won the 2020 election?" Donald Trump famously and frequently says that the election was stolen from him, but his new website plainly states that Joseph R. Biden Jr. won. The bot does sometimes tie the answer to the electoral count, stating that Biden won 306 votes to Trump's 232, but I was surprised to see "Joseph R. Biden Jr. won the 2020 presidential election under the official Electoral College count" as an answer on this site.

The site will also tell you that Donald Trump was president when diesel prices hit their highest historic price ($6.529 per gallon as of Sept. 21, 2026.), and that prices are high, in part, due to "military action" affecting the Staight of Hormuz. It will also say that grocery prices were higher in August than they were a year ago, which contradicts Trump's claims that prices have come down under his term.

Of course, Trump-influenced information that appears on official government sites will appear here. Ask it what the body of water that abuts Texas is called, and it will say the Gulf of America, formerly the Gulf of Mexico. Ask it what lake borders Toronto, Canada, and the bot will say Lake America, formerly Lake Ontario. In both cases, it will refer to the executive orders that changed those names.

Typically, I'd be worried about an AI tool hallucinating its answers and providing incorrect information to users. That's still a concern here, of course. But by creating a chatbot that only pulls information from official government sources, Trump has inadvertently created an official government fact-checker. And unless Trump starts injecting these sites with the same falsehoods he tells in interviews and on Truth Social, America.gov may be a reasonably reliable source of information.

fullText:
An ancient ground carving that was severely damaged by the administration’s border wall construction was created before Stonehenge and Egypt’s oldest pyramid, according to recently publicized research.

The Las Playas Intaglio, a giant fish carved into the Sonoran Desert in Arizona, is now considered the oldest example in the Americas of a geoglyphic, the ancient art form that is carved into or drawn on the ground.

In April, contractors hired by the Trump administration to make way for a second wall along the Arizona-Mexico border “scraped” a 50-foot swath through the ancient carving, according to the Center for Biological Diversity, which documented the damage.

The intaglio on the ground of the ancestral homeland of the Tohono O’odham and other Indigenous tribes is estimated to be about 2,000 years older than Egypt’s first pyramid and to have been created about 1,500 years before the first construction of Stonehenge and 4,000 years before Peru’s Nazca Lines, researchers have found.

The formerly 272-foot carving had originally been thought to be about 1,000 years old. But the latest research dates the art’s creation to at least 6,500 years ago, and possibly as much as 7,500 years ago.

That age emphasizes “the significance of this site and the parallel great misfortune resulting from its damage,” the researchers said in an article published in The SAA Archaeological Record.

“This discovery makes an already devastating loss even more profound. It’s a cultural and historical atrocity,” Russ McSpadden, Southwest conservation advocate at the Center for Biological Diversity, said in a statement.

A Customs and Border Protection spokesperson said in an email to NBC News that the contractor “inadvertently disturbed” the site and that CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott has been “engaged directly with tribal leadership to determine appropriate next steps.”

“The remaining portion of the site has been secured and will be protected in place. CBP is conducting a thorough review of construction protocols and strengthening communication procedures to ensure this does not happen again,” the spokesperson stated, adding that the agency is “committed to respecting and safeguarding cultural heritage throughout all border infrastructure projects.”

The damage to that site and construction on other parts of Tohono O’odham land and sacred Indigenous areas has strained the tenuous relationship between the tribal nation and the government. The tribe is appealing a federal judge’s decision refusing to block the administration’s border wall construction through its reservation.

While the intaglio’s site is irreparably damaged, the Tohono O’odham people are trying to stop the government from plowing through Quitobaquito Springs, a desert water source in Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument that is also considered a sacred site and holds endangered species.

In order to build the border wall and barriers, the Department of Homeland Security invoked authority granted in the Secure Fence Act of 2006 to waive numerous laws protecting the environment, water, cultural, historical and religious sites.

The Tohono O’odham Nation has long worked with CBP, which is part of the Department of Homeland Security, on border security, helping to keep drug traffickers and others from using its land for criminal activity.

The tribe’s reservation straddles the U.S.-Mexico border, and its members have permission to move between the two countries with ID checks. About 3,000 of its members are in Mexico, according to the tribal nation.

The Center for Biological Diversity stated in a news release that conservation advocates and tribal nations have long warned that border wall and secondary border barrier plans could cut through sensitive habitat and cultural sites across the region.

Wall construction in other parts of the border has sparked other lawsuits and opposition from landowners, Native American tribes, local governments, conservation groups, business owners and others.

In Texas, a tribal nonprofit for the Lipan Apache and an outdoor recreation business have opposed the border wall construction, alleging DHS is not authorized to violate the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, which they say it would do by destroying or cutting off access to sacred sites.

A federal judge ordered a temporary halt to construction in Big Bend National Park in response to the lawsuit, but construction continues on other parts of the rugged, undeveloped and remote region outside state and federal parkland.

fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Department of Homeland Security has tapped $20 million to pay for the campaign-style ads glorifying President Donald Trump that have drawn widespread criticism from Republicans and Democrats as a blatant misuse of taxpayer dollars that likely runs afoul of anti-propaganda law.

In a letter Tuesday to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, two top Democratic senators said that the money is being drawn from Trump's so-called "One Big Beautiful Bill" and was supposed to go for U.S. Customs and Border Protection.

"We should not have to remind you that using government funding to create or air political ads like the ones that have been running over the last few days is illegal and a shockingly corrupt misuse of taxpayer dollars," wrote Sen. Patty Murray of Washington, the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, and Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut, the ranking Democrat on the subcommittee that handles Homeland Security funding.

The senators demanded answers within the next 48 hours about "how this president is literally stealing their tax dollars to air campaign ads celebrating himself."

They asked the secretary if the department plans to use additional federal funds to air these ads or create new ones, and if so to share contracting information with Congress. They also asked Mullin if he had spoken to Trump about using the taxpayer funds for the ads.

The political uproar over Trump's hagiographic ads, which started running last week during popular TV shows, including college and National Football League programming, has not abated as critics on the left and right raise alarms about the use of taxpayer funds, particularly so close to the midterm elections.

The White House has defended the advertisements, which disclose that they are funded by the U.S. government, as public service announcements.

Asked for a request for comment Tuesday on the senators' letter, Homeland Security referred to the earlier White House response.

The unusual commercials, which echo the GOP's midterm election slogans, against imagery of Trump's tenure in office — one with a "Love me, Love me" song refrain in the background — appear to violate a law against congressionally appropriated funds being used for propaganda.

Experts also have said the ads, which are airing on network and cable TV and streaming, differ from other administrations' PSAs because they aren't designed to help Americans access any specific program.

Over the weekend, a new ad promoting the president resembles a black-and-white video from his own 2024 campaign that shows Trump walking down a hallway as his voice can be heard warning of a "final battle" against "globalists" and "warmongers." It ends with Trump staring straight into the camera lens with the "Paid for by the U.S. Government" message printed.

Sen. Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, has compared Trump's ads to those used by authoritarian former leader Viktor Orban of Hungary. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a Republican from South Dakota, said it "shouldn't be paid for with taxpayer dollars."

Data from the outside firm AdImpact shows more than $2.5 million was spent on the three ads over the past seven days. The actual amount spent could be significantly more, depending on whether networks classified the ads as political.

The senators said in their letter that DHS has committed $20 million to the campaign.

A person who was not authorized to discuss the situation and who was granted anonymity confirmed the findings, which were first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

The unusual ad campaign comes as Republicans face an increasingly volatile midterm election season with their control of the House and Senate — and Trump's future agenda — all at risk.

Voters say they are struggling with high prices of gas and groceries, and are concerned about the lengthy U.S. war against Iran, now in its seventh month. Democrats are gearing up for vast oversight of Trump and his administration if they seize power, and impeachment is not off the table.

House Democrats said Trump's director of the Office of Management and Budget, Russ Vought, moved $20 million from Homeland Security resources to the ad campaign on Sept. 19.

The next day, a $20 million contract for a "National Media Campaign" was awarded to the Maryland-based LMD Agency, Inc., according to federal data. LMD Agency did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Homeland Security funds are part of a whopping $175 billion Congress gave the department in the "Big, Beautiful, Bill" as part of Trump's immigration enforcement and deportation agenda. Democrats voted against that package, which Trump signed into law last summer, in part because of its steep cuts to Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, known as SNAP.

Rep. Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, and Rep. Henry Cuellar of Texas, the ranking Democrat on the Homeland Security subcommittee, said that after gutting $1 trillion from Medicaid and social services and "more than quadrupling funding for mass deportations, it turns out the Trump administration used Republicans' One Big Beautiful Bill to pay for President Trump's political ads."

They said if the Democrats regain control, they "will work to uncover and reverse misuses of taxpayer money like this and hold those who abused their power accountable."

What's also striking about the administration's use of taxpayer dollars for the ads is that Trump's own political campaign committee, MAGA Inc., is sitting on hundreds of millions of dollars of funding that could be used during the midterm season. Groups aligned with MAGA Inc. have started shelling out funds for the House and Senate races.

The administration has defended the use of taxpayer dollars for the ads and shown no signs of changing course.

title: Jack Smith defends Trump probes as GOP senators grill him over subpoenas: 5 takeaways
description:
Former special counsel Jack Smith fielded insults from Republicans and questions about his prosecutorial decisions as he sat before lawmakers on the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday.

fullText:
Former special counsel Jack Smith fielded insults from Republicans and questions about his prosecutorial decisions as he sat before lawmakers on the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday.

Chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) has been a leading voice in scrutinizing Smith’s twin probes into President Trump, obtaining and releasing reams of documents about the investigations while criticizing his decision to subpoena some lawmakers’ call logs.

Smith defended his work, saying Trump faced criminal charges related to the Mar-a-Lago classified documents case and the case tied to the president’s role in the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol as a result of his own illegal conduct. He added that he would have brought charges against any president who committed such crimes.

Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), meanwhile, accused the GOP of “gaslighting” the American public about how damaging the Jan. 6 attack was to democracy.

But Smith largely served as a punching bag for the committee’s Republicans.

“You may think you’re a hero in this story, but let me tell you something. You’re the villain. You’ve done so much damage,” Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) told Smith.

“You will go down as a total dirtbag.”

Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) said Smith’s probe “makes what Richard Nixon did in Watergate look like a Sunday picnic.” Here are five takeaways from Tuesday’s fiery Senate hearing.

Smith obtained the call logs of a dozen Republican senators as part of his investigation into Jan. 6 — and Tuesday was their first chance to press him on the supboenas.

Smith described toll records, which are essentially call logs, as “noncontent records” that were important for mapping out communication among different parties.

“Those records corroborated evidence that we had that the president, President Donald Trump, and his co-conspirators were seeking to exploit the violence on Jan. 6 in furtherance of their criminal scheme,” Smith said.

“It was an important part of our investigation, and it was centrally relevant to the issue of criminal intent to seek to further delay the proceedings in violation of the law, given what had happened that afternoon at Jan. 6, in my view, added to the powerful evidence we had of Donald Trump’s guilt, and the participation of his co-conspirators in his criminal scheme at his behest.”

But Republicans on the panel accused Smith of violating the Speech or Debate Clause, as well as their privacy, saying he should not have sought a gag order barring cellphone companies from disclosing the move.

Smith said he consulted Department of Justice (DOJ) experts on the constitutional limitations and got approval to pursue the records.

“You subpoenaed records associated with my phones, both personal and office, and you sought and obtained a court order to prevent me from knowing about it. For years, you were able to ask your questions in secret without me in the room. Today, the Senate gets to ask questions,” Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) said.

“You willingly were conscripted as a foot soldier for the DNC [Democratic National Committee] and you know what you also did. You reelected President Donald Trump because the American people were disgusted at your willingness to abuse power in partisan ends.”

Smith said the records showed Trump’s efforts to coordinate with lawmakers to delay certification as well as those who contacted the White House in alarm.

“We gained evidence [of people] reaching out to the White House, asking, ‘Please help us. Please stop what’s happening. Please have your supporters stop attacking the Capitol,’” Smith said.

The GOP’s subpoena outrage wasn’t just limited to collection of call records but numerous compulsory demands for Republican-affiliated groups.

“In all, you issued 197 subpoenas to 34 individuals at least, and 163 businesses, and you sought records on at least 430 Republican individuals and entities,” Cruz said. “If you look at the list, there is one thing that is consistent. Every name on it is a Republican.”

Smith said the team had to follow the money to map out the financial backing for a number of groups that sponsored and organized events surrounding election challenges as well as Trump’s Jan. 6, 2021, speech on the Ellipse.

“I can tell you why we issued subpoenas, and it was to conduct a criminal investigation of one of the most serious crimes that’s ever happened in our nation’s history. I had a duty to collect facts,” Smith said.

“We had to conduct an investigation about whether any person or entity violated the law with respect to the attempt to block the peaceful transfer of power, to make that decision.”

Grassley, who first revealed the subpoenas, was not convinced.

“No matter what you say, there is no legitimate basis for what you did, especially since your staff killed an investigation into the [Hillary] Clinton campaign. Donations to Republican groups wasn’t necessary for your investigation, which is proved out by the fact that it was not mentioned in your public report,” the lawmaker said.

Smith in his opening statement said the blame for criminal charges lies at Trump’s feet and was not motivated by politics.

“The charges against President Trump were the result of the evidence. Grand juries in two separate districts reached this conclusion based on his actions, as alleged in the indictments they returned,” Smith said in his opening statements.

“Our investigation developed proof beyond a reasonable doubt that President Trump engaged in criminal activity. If asked whether to prosecute a former president based on the same facts today, I would do so regardless of whether that president was a Republican or a Democrat.”

The former prosecutor also stood up for his staff, most of whom were fired from the Trump-led DOJ given their association with the investigation.

“These are people who stood sentry for us, experts in national security, experts in corruption investigations, who were simply fired because they worked on the wrong case — that has never happened in my career. I have never seen anything remotely like it in any Republican or Democratic administration,” Smith said.

When asked later by Cruz whether he had any regrets, Smith retorted, “I regret that the people I worked with have been unfairly fired and vilified.”

One of the most widely discussed moments of the hearing came as Schmitt pressed Smith about whether he attended an Atlanta Hawks basketball game in February 2024.

Smith was clearly confused by the question, and then Schmitt provided more context, noting that the basketball game would have fallen the day after Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis (D) in Georgia acknowledged dating one of her staffers — a drama-filled development in the state-level case against Trump.

Smith later volunteered he had attended an Iowa Hawkeyes game in Maryland, saying he had wanted to see Caitlin Clark play.

Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), who was next in line for questioning, posited that Schmitt may have confused the Atlanta Hawks with the Iowa Hawkeyes.

“Could it then be that University of Iowa is the Hawkeyes? … That might be the confusion over the names of the team,” she said.

The question led to heated moments between Schmitt and the committee’s Democrats — who noted that his staff swiftly swept away text messages printed on a poster that appeared to reference stadium seat numbers.

Schmitt later relented and placed the poster up for Smith’s response.

It’s unclear what Schmitt’s goal was in seeking out whether Smith had ever been to Atlanta.

During his questioning, Smith said he never met Willis.

Schmitt fumed at Klobuchar for igniting an “open session” about his questions and accused her of “trying to rehabilitate the witness.”

“I presented him with text messages about him wanting to meet with people that could have obviously been related to the prosecution that was coordinated with his office in Atlanta,” Schmitt said.

Smith said he planned to call a number of GOP witnesses had the case further progressed in court, telling Sen. Darlene Graham (R-S.C.) he perhaps would have called her brother to testify.

The comment came as Graham questioned why Smith sought phone records of her late brother, former Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).

“I believe your brother was a patriotic public servant. He was not a target of our investigation, and in fact, he likely would have been a witness in our case. Your brother investigated the claims that Donald Trump was making. He found them to be false,” Smith said, before Darlene Graham cut short his kudos.

Smith also said he regretted not offering more public statements while the case was ongoing, agreeing with Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) that the DOJ has to be open with the public to build support for the legitimacy of its work.

“One of the things that I was taught as a prosecutor through my career is you only do your talking in the courtroom, and that you don’t talk on the courthouse steps,” he said in response to a question from Tillis.

“One of the things that I learned from this experience is that if you stick to that and that alone, people can unfairly malign your team, and unfairly malign you and your case in a way, and you really can’t respond because you don’t want to interfere with someone’s right to a fair trial.”

Donald Trump and Australian golfer Adam Scott shared an extended handshake at Medinah on Sunday, according to Yahoo Sports. Scott appeared to pull away before Trump released his grip, and both men seemed to smile.

Trump used his signature grab-and-tug move as Scott approached, then leaned in to speak quietly into the golfer's ear. Scott then went on his way afterward, according to AOL and Irish Star reports.

White House physician reports from 2018 and 2019 list Donald Trump at 6 feet 3 inches. The 2019 report, released after his exam at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center, was covered by NBC News.

Trump served as honorary chairman at the 2017 Presidents Cup at Liberty National Golf Club in Jersey City, New Jersey. He became the first sitting U.S. president to present the trophy, according to Yahoo Sports.

He is honorary chairman again in 2026 as the 47th U.S. president. His honorary position has traditionally been held by a leader of the host country. Australian Prime Minister Scott Morrison held the role when the Presidents Cup was played in Melbourne in 2019.

Team USA beat the International Team 17 to 13 at Medinah Country Club to win the 2026 Presidents Cup. It was the 14th American victory overall and the 11th in a row, according to GolfMagic.

Brandt Snedeker placed several of his strongest players early in the Sunday singles lineup. The goal was to give the United States a fast start on the scoreboard. The Americans went on to win 9.5 of the 12 available singles points.

After the victory, Snedeker said his team never lost faith despite entering Sunday three points behind. He also referenced Medinah's history of dramatic comebacks, including the 2012 Ryder Cup. Snedeker played for the U.S. team that lost to Europe there in 2012.

Adam Scott played in his 12th consecutive Presidents Cup in 2026, tying Phil Mickelson's record. The 46-year-old Australian made his Presidents Cup debut in 2003 at age 23. That International Team also included Ernie Els and Retief Goosen.

fullText:
Apparent confusion over team names derailed a line of questioning as Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) grilled former special counsel Jack Smith on Tuesday about his attendance at a basketball game, suggesting the prosecutor may have coordinated with others bringing charges about President Trump.

The exchange would later prompt Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii) to say the panel had been "witness to a narrative, a false narrative of accusing [Smith] of being at a game that you were nowhere near, and I suppose that was supposed to be in furtherance of some sort of conspiracy."

Schmitt asked Smith if he had traveled to Atlanta in 2024 to watch an Atlanta Hawks basketball game, alluding to the trip as a chance to meet Fani Willis, the top prosecutor in the city. Willis also brought charges against Trump.

Schmitt said he had texts referencing the game, though a board displaying the messages was only briefly shown by the senator's staff.

Schmitt seemed surprised when Smith said he did not recall going to Atlanta during that time period and also said he did not meet Willis. For his part, Smith seemed puzzled.

"I really don't think so. It's possible I flew through the Atlanta airport on the way to Florida, but I do not have a recollection of going to Atlanta. I definitely did not go to a Hawks game," Smith said.

The significance of the trip from Schmitt's perspective was that the February 2024 game he referenced was the day after Willis revealed she was in a relationship with one of her own staffers, sparking a firestorm of scrutiny around the already high-profile Fulton County election interference case.

"Let me just give you a little context. The day before Fani Willis came clean with her affair with the prosecutor, you know, the Atlanta prosecutor that was also trying to get Trump. The next day, were you in Atlanta?" Schmitt asked.

Smith said he had at one point attended an Iowa Hawkeyes game in Maryland, as he wanted to watch Caitlin Clark play.

Schmitt's questioning ended with the lawmaker calling Smith a "villain" and "dirtbag."

Amid protests from Democrats, Schmitt initially refused to again show the text messages he displayed on the board, prompting some to say Smith deserved to see what he was being asked to respond to. Schmitt later relented.

The text messages show one prosecutor on Smith's team having booked a meeting room only to be told by another staffer that Smith is "already down here." The text messages he displayed don't reference any basketball team names or games, though Schmitt at one point told Smith, "I don't think you know that we have this stuff."

Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), who was next in line for questioning, posited that Schmitt may have confused the Atlanta Hawks with the Iowa Hawkeyes.

"Could it then be that University of Iowa is the Hawkeyes? … That might be the confusion over the names of the team," she said.

"That might be the confusion over the names of the team. But perhaps you should have looked at it more carefully."

Schmitt then snapped that Klobuchar was trying to "rehabilitate the witness."

After wrapping her questioning, Klobuchar criticized Schmitt for calling the prosecutor a "dirtbag."

"We have confirmed that, in fact, you are right, Mr. Smith. Iowa, the Iowa Hawkeyes, played Maryland on Feb. 3, 2024. The final score was 93 to 85. Iowa won, and Caitlin Clark scored over 30 points, so it must have been a pretty good game. The game was, in fact, in Maryland, Mr. Smith," she said.

"And I would just say, for a U.S. senator to have false information and imply, based on a confusion about the name of a team, which I knew, knowing my Midwestern sports, and imply that you were in another city that you were somehow involved that day in what was happening in Georgia and then call you a dirtbag is something that deserves an apology."

fullText:
President Donald Trump has personally driven the controversial, taxpayer-funded video ads promoting himself and his administration’s policies, including helping select the imagery and videos used, a source familiar with the matter told CNN.

Two Trump advisers familiar with the ads said that they were being created in-house by the White House video team — which is part of the communications team, responsible for the administration’s public messaging.

Coming just over a month before the November midterms, the ads have generated bipartisan criticism over how the Trump administration is spending taxpayer dollars.

“It’s a great message. I like the message, but it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters in the Capitol on Monday.

GOP Sen. John Cornyn of Texas echoed that sentiment: “It’s not even a close question.”

The White House has broadly defended the ads, saying they are akin to public service announcements past administrations have put out about Medicare, Obamacare and Covid-19 vaccinations. Officials have insisted they “are very clearly not campaign ads.”

“These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad,” a White House spokesperson said Monday.

But the imagery is undeniably meant to promote Trump, casting him as a warrior battling against existential threats. And the latest one appears nearly identical to a video Trump posted on Truth Social in January 2024, during his third presidential campaign.

That most recent ad shows Trump walking down a hall as audio plays of him saying “this is the final battle.”

“We will cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists. We will throw off the sick political class that hates our country. We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all,” Trump says in the ad, echoing comments he made during a Veterans Day speech in 2023.

The version on Truth Social has an additional six seconds that includes Trump’s campaign logo and a number to text. The text “Paid for by the US Government” is seen across the screen at the end of the new version of the ad.

Multiple members of Trump’s political operation said they were unaware that these ads were coming until they aired. But another source pushed back on the notion that anyone was kept in the dark — noting that the president had spoken about the ads to multiple aides and advisers and insisting that they were not being made in secret.

The latest ad — which aired during at least two NFL games on Sunday, during Fox’s broadcasts of the Washington Commanders-Seattle Seahawks matchup as well as the Carolina Panthers-Cleveland Browns game — is the third government-funded message in recent days to be captured by the media tracker AdImpact.

An ad that began airing Wednesday featured rapidly edited pictures and video of Trump over audio of him denouncing communism and socialism. Text on the screen touted his administration’s accomplishments, including “reigniting American manufacturing.”

“The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic,” a White House spokesperson said in a statement. “We should be proud of our country.”

The music used in that ad — a song called “Love Me” by JMSN — has also come under scrutiny. Lawyers for the artist sent White House chief of staff Susie Wiles a letter on Monday asking the administration to “immediately withdraw the advertisement from all scheduled airings” and “cease and desist any use of the Song and/or any of the intellectual property of JMSN.”

A second ad features video of Trump at Mount Rushmore as his voice is heard saying, “Never before has any nation celebrated so magnificent a triumph as this one.”

Beyond questions of intellectual property, watchdog groups say the ads mark a clear violation of appropriations law restricting the use of federal funding for propaganda or partisan communications.

“The most immediate check on this kind of behavior is supposed to be and needs to be Congress. Congress has not asserted itself as the first branch of government with the power of the purse to hold the president accountable,” said Donald Sherman, president and CEO of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics, or CREW, in Washington.

GOP lawmakers may be hesitant to provide accountability, he added, because the ads “are designed to boost Republicans in Congress,” he said.

And, Sherman noted, the Government Accountability Office — the nonpartisan agency that would be tasked with investigations into this type of issue — is currently without Senate-confirmed leadership.

“That makes it that much harder for them to move with speed to address a high-profile and politically sensitive investigation like this requires,” he said.

Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, said in a post on X that the ads “may be felony criminal theft and conversion of government property for political campaign purposes.”

And Raskin, who will gain congressional subpoena power in November if Democrats win the House, said it is not just Trump who might face inquiries over the messages. He said the creation of the ads was a “Hatch Act violation for any government employees who worked on it or used government resources to make it.”

“This is dumb, dumb, dumb beyond belief,” one former Trump campaign official told CNN. “These guys are all gonna get subpoenaed. It’s gonna be bad.”

The story has been updated with additional information.

CNN’s Kit Maher contributed to this report.

Murphy's ruling came in a class-action lawsuit filed by immigrant rights groups on behalf of migrants seeking to prevent the US government from sending them to third countries without notice and a chance to assert the harms they could face.

More than 25,000 migrants have been deported to 29 countries under the policy implemented last year, according to a tally by human rights groups, with the vast majority going to Mexico.

The policy is one of a number of measures the administration has taken in its pursuit of Trump's goal of mass deportation. The Republican president has enforced ‌a sweeping crackdown on immigration — among his top priorities — since returning ⁠to office last year.

The administration has carried out third-country deportations to politically unstable South Sudan, which the US State Department urges Americans to avoid due to the risks of crime, kidnapping and armed conflict, as well as Uganda, Equatorial Guinea, Liberia, the Central African Republic, and other nations.

Department of Homeland Security General ⁠Counsel James Percival welcomed the court's decision.

"A bad day for criminal illegals and open-borders activists alike," Percival wrote on social media.

Trina Realmuto, a lawyer for the plaintiffs at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, said the court has "allowed the administration to resume sending people to third countries where they face persecution or torture. That is a devastating result for people who may be put on a plane before they ever have notice or an ​opportunity ​to raise a fear claim."

In February, Murphy ruled that the policy violates immigration law procedures and due process ​protections under the US Constitution's Fifth Amendment. Due process generally requires the government ‌to provide notice and an opportunity for a hearing before taking certain adverse actions.

The Supreme Court, which has allowed a number of Trump's hardline immigration policies, previously sided with the administration in the legal challenge, suspending a preliminary order that Murphy issued earlier in the case halting the removals. In another win for the administration, the Supreme Court subsequently lifted limits the judge had imposed to protect a group of men from being sent to South Sudan.

The case began in 2025 after the Department of Homeland Security moved to step up deportations of migrants who cannot be returned to any country listed on their deportation orders.

The policy provided that migrants could be swiftly removed without notice to third countries that have provided credible diplomatic assurance that they will not persecute or torture the individuals. ‌For countries that have not provided such assurance, deportees would be notified of their destination and US authorities ​would assess the likelihood of persecution or torture only if the individual raises such fear on their own.

In its emergency ​filing to the Supreme Court, the Justice Department said third-country deportations are "an essential tool to ​remove certain aliens, including some of the worst criminal aliens."

But both Murphy and critics of the administration said the policy is also targeting migrants who had ‌been granted legal protection from being sent back to their home countries.

The ​policy has resulted in deportees being unlawfully transferred by ​third countries back to their home countries from which the US had already granted them protection, while others have been beaten, sexually assaulted, detained or have disappeared, the plaintiffs said in a court filing.

The administration is ignoring "the significant harm resulting from deporting thousands of longtime US residents, many with no criminal history, to third countries without regard to the persecution ​or torture they face there," the plaintiffs said.

The Boston-based 1st US Circuit ‌Court of Appeals upheld most of the judge's ruling on September 18.

The case has been hotly contested since it began, and included findings by Murphy that the administration "repeatedly ​violated, or attempted to violate" his orders. Murphy in 2025 found that the administration had violated another order he issued requiring additional steps before attempting to send ​a group of migrants to South Sudan.

fullText:
President Trump gathered top artificial intelligence leaders in Washington on Tuesday and doubled down on his opposition to government intervention, suggesting that "self-regulation" is the answer to growing worries about the technology getting out of human control.

"There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation," the president said after meeting with the assembled CEOs. "There was a lot of commonality in this room."

Trump said he and the CEOs signed a "morally binding" accord that wasn't immediately released but that the president said would keep the companies in line through "self-policing and group policing."

Some executives on hand said the so-called Accord on Super Intelligence would include commitments to a combination of technological controls to detect problems with new models, internal risk review efforts, external auditors, and other measures.

Meta (META) CEO Mark Zuckerberg called the accord "a start," while others suggested some details still needed to be worked out.

"The mechanism, how we address those risks, is still under discussion," Anthropic (ANTH.PVT) CEO Dario Amodei said. Progress had been made toward both the US winning AI and also winning safely, he said, though he emphasized that the technology still poses "real dangers."

Amodei published an essay earlier this month titled "We Must Pace the Frontier," which set off a fierce debate about the need for a cooperative slowdown in AI capability.

The accord also formally changed the name of the technology in government record-keeping to Super Intelligence.

"We've changed the name officially to SI," Trump said.

The "meeting and luncheon on Super Intelligence," as the White House described the event, took place in the East Room, with Trump even posting the seating chart. The location was the same spot where just a few days ago, many of the same AI leaders gathered for a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Elon Musk of Tesla (TSLA), Jensen Huang of Nvidia (NVDA), and Lisa Su of Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) were all at the head table with Xi last Thursday and again received prominent spots near Trump.

After the meeting, Trump also said he was "very close" to a decision on an AI czar and would announce it in the next three to four days.

Other notable guests included Google (GOOGL, GOOG) CEO Sundar Pichai, Microsoft (MSFT) CEO Satya Nadella, OpenAI (OPAI.PVT) president Greg Brockman, Palantir (PLTR) CEO Alex Karp, Amazon (AMZN) founder Jeff Bezos, and others.

The gathering came as the US continues to digest a raft of alarming new AI disclosures in recent days, such as an Axios report that OpenAI, Anthropic, and security researchers were sifting through thousands of incidents of problematic actions by AI agents.

fullText:
President Donald Trump launched America.gov on Tuesday, unveiling what the administration has billed as a new AI-powered gateway to federal information and services that aims to streamline Americans' interactions with the government.

The website, which Trump introduced at Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium in Washington, features a chatbot-style interface that allows users to ask questions about government programs, benefits and services. The administration described America.gov as a "front door" to federal resources, consolidating information that is currently spread across dozens of agency websites.

"It's not just simply a website. It's a restoration of America's founding promise, and it's a reinvention of your government for the 21st century and beyond," Trump said at the rollout.

The debut of America.gov comes as policymakers, technology companies and privacy advocates continue to debate the expanding role of artificial intelligence in public-facing services. While AI tools have been touted for their ability to simplify complex tasks and improve access to information, experts have raised concerns about accuracy, transparency and data privacy, particularly when such systems are used to help people access government programs or services.

Asked at the announcement about risks associated with AI and centralized government services, Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz told Newsweek the administration does not want all user data stored in a single location. Instead, he described America.gov as a "federated system" in which individuals maintain control of their own records and choose whether to share them. Oz acknowledged that any system allowing access to sensitive information carries risks, but said federal officials are prioritizing cybersecurity and data protection as the platform evolves.

"We don't want all the information in one link," Oz said. "The real risk we have is if all your data is in one spot ... anyone who hacks it gets it all."

The president said Tuesday, "It cannot in theory be hacked into. And when they figure a way to do that, we'll end it, because they always figure a way, right?"

Joe Gebbia, U.S. chief design officer, said America.gov is powered by Google's Gemini and Elon Musk's Grok. Trump was joined by Musk, administration officials and tech leaders for the announcement.

Newsweek has reached out to the White House via email on Tuesday morning for comment.

Trump signed an executive order Tuesday that directs federal agencies to integrate their online services with America.gov, which the administration envisions as a single digital portal for accessing government information and completing transactions.

The White House said the platform will eventually allow users to perform tasks such as renewing passports and enrolling in Medicare, while Login.gov, the federal government's existing sign-in system, will be incorporated into the service.

The order applies to public-facing federal services used by more than 100,000 people annually, although IRS tax-filing services and certain national security-related functions are excluded.

"This is the American government working for the American people. Come to America.gov, tell us what you need. We'll help you get there and, ultimately, we'll help you get it done," Edward Frost, Administrator of the U.S. General Services Administration (GSA), told Newsweek at Tuesday's announcement.

The launch of America.gov also highlights the growing influence of Gebbia, the Airbnb co-founder whom Trump tapped in 2025 to lead the newly created National Design Studio. Established under the administration's "America by Design" initiative, the office is responsible for modernizing federal websites and digital services.

The chatbot-based America.gov portal represents one of the most visible examples of Gebbia's effort to apply Silicon Valley-style design principles to the federal government.

The launch of America.gov coincides with a high-profile White House gathering of some of the technology industry's most influential executives.

Trump will host a lunch focused on AI shortly after unveiling the new portal Attendees include Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora and Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner.

The technology leaders joined Vice President JD Vance, House Speaker Mike Johnson, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. The meeting comes as artificial intelligence is playing an increasingly prominent role in both the private and public sectors, with governments around the world grappling with how to harness the technology while addressing concerns about accuracy, privacy and security.

Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here.

Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gabe Whisnant and Dave Siminoff.

title: Iranian spokesman urges Americans to rally against Trump's policies in address
description: Iran's Revolutionary Guard urged Americans in a message ahead of U.S. midterm elections to take to the streets and rally against Donald Trump, claiming the U.S. president's war in the Middle East has failed.
fullText:
Iran's Revolutionary Guard urged Americans in a message ahead of U.S. midterm elections to take to the streets and rally against Donald Trump, claiming the U.S. president's war in the Middle East has failed.

Meanwhile, in the occupied West Bank, settlers rioted, throwing rocks, blocking roads and setting Palestinian property on fire to prevent a Palestinian man escorted by the Israeli military from returning to his home in the village of Jalud.

Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Tuesday. Full coverage is available here.

Gen. Hossein Mohebbi, spokesman for the Revolutionary Guard, held a news conference in Tehran, Iran's capital, on Tuesday and read from what he said was a "letter to the American people."

Reading from the prepared text, he said that the only way for the war to end is for Washington to admit defeat and leave. The message was apparently meant for the U.S. public just weeks ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections for the U.S. Senate and Congress — a vote in which Trump's Republican Party faces fierce headwinds as it looks to maintain control of Congress.

Later, in remarks to The Associated Press, Mohebbi urged Americans to take to the streets and protest Trump's policies to denounce what he called the U.S. government's war-mongering policies.

Mohebbi also said Americans should "revise their decision" about their leaders.

He accused the United States of using Iran's nuclear program as a ruse to "plunder Iran's wealth" and to turn the country "back into a colony." The U.S. military action and economic sanctions would not get Tehran to submit.

Meanwhile, Iran's currency fell to a new record low Tuesday, with traders in Tehran exchanging more than 2.5 million rials to the U.S. dollar, a sign of how the conflict has further eroded Iran's economy.

The decline came after the rial hit its previous record low of 2.2 million to the dollar on Sept. 2. The currency has repeatedly reached new lows since the war began in February.

Over a hundred Israeli settlers scuffled with Israeli soldiers who were trying to escort a Palestinian man to his home in the West Bank village of Jalud.

The homeowner, Mahmoud Tubasi, told the AP that the soldiers initially brought him to his home but that rioting settlers forced him to leave with his family in a military vehicle. He said he still can't access the house, which settlers have besieged for two months.

Israel's military acknowledged that the overnight mission to return the family "was not completed" and that three officers were injured by settlers who threw rocks, blocked roads and set Palestinian property on fire.

Israeli police said they arrested three settlers suspected of participating in the riot, which was condemned by Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Foreign Minister Gidon Saar and President Isaac Herzog.

The Israeli military has struggled to quell the latest wave of settler violence. Rights groups have accused the military of colluding with the settlers.

An Israeli strike on an apartment west of Gaza City killed two people, including a Hamas commander who the Israeli military said was involved in plotting attacks and recruiting new members for the militant group.

Al-Shifa Hospital officials said Tuesday the strike also wounded five others.

Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz said the overnight strike targeted Izz al-Din Bik, a commander in the Hamas militant group's northern Gaza brigade.

Hamas confirmed the death of al-Bik, claiming in a statement he was one of the main overseers of the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks on southern Israel, which killed over 1,200 and prompted the war in Gaza.

More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed since a ceasefire took effect nearly a year ago, according to Gaza's Health Ministry, while over 74,000 Palestinians have been killed since the war began. The ministry maintains detailed records that are generally seen as reliable. It does not distinguish between civilians and militants, but says women and children make up around half of the fatalities.

A mass funeral was held Tuesday in Gaza's Nuseirat refugee camp for nearly 50 people killed during the war.

The remains, wrapped in white bags and draped with Palestinian flags, were recovered last week from the rubble of buildings destroyed almost three years ago.

Mass funerals have become more common in Gaza, where Israel has not allowed the heavy machinery needed to clear the rubble of destroyed buildings and recover the dead.

Earlier this month, the United Nations estimated that more than 8,000 bodies remain buried under the debris.

For some, partial remains were all they had to bury.

Areej Farajallah said two of her husband's bones were found last week. She is also mourning her child, who was among those buried Tuesday.

Abdel-Nasser al-Tawil said his home was hit Oct. 15, 2023, in the early days of the war. He said he recovered 13 bodies Tuesday with the help of the Red Cross and Palestinian Civil Defense workers ahead of the funeral.

This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.

fullText:
President Trump’s new government-funded ads pledging to “cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists” are getting strong pushback from Senate Republicans who are warning the president not to use taxpayer money to promote himself in such a brazenly political way.

While Republicans generally approve of Trump’s political message, they say using taxpayer dollars to fund a series of ads that closely resemble Trump’s past campaign advertising right before the midterm elections is inappropriate.

“It’s a great message, I like the message, but it shouldn’t be paid for by taxpayer dollars,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) told reporters Monday.

The White House, however, argues the ads — which ran over the weekend during “Fox News Sunday” and several college and NFL football games — are “very clearly not campaign ads” and instead “a reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it’s worth defending.”

Republican senators are not buying that argument, and warn that it creates an improper appearance to be using taxpayer money to pay for television ads that could easily be confused with regular campaign ads, even though Trump himself is not on the ballot.

“It would not have been something that I would have done,” said Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.). “I know that the White House is not covered by the same guidance that we are, but it’s not something I would have done.”

“I just don’t think it’s right to be using taxpayer money in that way, particularly if it’s tied to political campaigns,” he added. “I think they need to rethink that strategy.”

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) said using taxpayer money to fund a television ad that’s nearly identical to the ad that Trump posted to social media during his presidential campaign and echoes the rhetoric he has used at election-year rallies crosses a red line.

“We all know you’re not supposed to use taxpayer money for that purpose,” the Republican senator noted.

Cornyn said he doesn’t know exactly where the money to produce and air the ads is coming from but added “if it comes from taxpayers, it shouldn’t.”

The latest advertisement, which ran on television over the weekend, is part of a series of ads that come with the disclaimer: “Paid by the U.S. Government.”

It is nearly identical to an online ad that Trump posted to his Truth Social account in January 2024, when he was preparing to launch his presidential campaign. In that online ad, he urged supporters to text “TRUMP to 88022” to support his campaign.

The ad features Trump walking down hallway while an audio clip plays of a speech he delivered at an unidentified event pledging: “This is the final battle. With you at my side, we will demolish the deep state, we will expel the warmongers from our government. We will drive out the globalists, we will cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists.”

“We will liberate America from these villains once and for all,” Trump is heard declaring as an unseen audience cheers in the background.

The latest iteration of the ad, however, ends with a disclaimer informing viewers that it was “paid for by the U.S. government.”

The White House aired its first ad of the new series last week — a 30-second television spot that featured a montage of pictures of the president, interspersed with Trump’s declaration that “together we will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America” and that “America will never be a communist country.”

The ad was paired with the song “Love Me” by JMSN and ended with a voiceover of UFC President Dana White extolling Trump as the “toughest, most resilient person I have ever met.”

The White House responded to criticisms in a statement.

“The attacks on President Donald J. Trump’s public service announcements are highly dishonest. The announcements are very clearly not campaign ads; President Trump is not on the ballot and there is no call to action,” the White House argued.

The White House noted that the George W. Bush administration ran a national television campaign explaining the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act to seniors — one of former President Bush’s signature legislative accomplishments — in March 2004, when Bush was up for reelection later that year.

The White House also pointed out that the Obama administration used national advertising to promote subsidies under the Affordable Care Act (ACA) in 2015 and the start of open enrollment under the ACA in 2016.

Republican Sen. John Curtis (Utah) said constituents “are worried about affordability and they don’t want to be worried about how their taxpayer dollars are being spent.”

“If it were me as a senator, it would be a problem,” he said of using taxpayer money to fund ads that appear to be political in nature.

“I don’t know their rules as well as I know mine, but I know mine would prohibit that,” he added.

A Senate GOP aide who requested anonymity to discuss the matter said the new Trump promotional ads paid for by the federal government appear “very similar” in nature to the promotional ads that then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem ran last year to tout her leadership of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

Trump fired Noem after she was grilled about the expenditure of public funds for the promotional ad blitz, which was estimated to cost more than $220 million.

Republican Sen. John Kennedy (La.), a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee who challenged Noem over DHS’s advertising campaign in March, said he disagreed with the Trump administration’s use of public funds for the new series of ads.

“I don’t think any public official, including President Trump … should spend public money on private ads for themselves,” Kennedy said Sunday on CBS News’s “Face the Nation.”

“The White House sees it differently,” he added.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) called on the Justice Department to investigate whether the use of taxpayer money to pay for ads promoting rhetoric similar to what Trump has used at political events violates the law.

“There should be a full investigation because on its face it appears to be a violation of federal law,” she said.

“The Department of Justice, the folks that enforce federal law, should be the ones” to lead the investigation, she said.

“This is the problem when the attorney general says his duty of loyalty is not to the people of the United States but instead is to Donald Trump personally,” she added, referring to Attorney General Todd Blanche.

Richard Painter, a White House ethics lawyer who served under Bush, wrote on social platform X that the use of taxpayer money to promote the president’s political message shortly before the midterm election “could be an impeachable offense.”

“@POTUS has no right to use taxpayer money for campaign ads. Congress has expressly prohibited government sponsored political propaganda, which is dangerous for democracy,” he warned.
